title: Emor: appointed times (Leviticus 23)
hook: Shabbat, Passover, the Omer, Shavuot, the new year, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, all in one chapter

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, speak and say, doubled. Your line was the old teach the young. Did you pass one small thing on? Today, the chapter that builds the Jewish year. Day four hundred sixteen.

Open a Jewish calendar and you'll see two systems at once. The ordinary months, January, February. And, printed smaller, Hebrew months with names like Nisan and Tishrei, and holidays that wander across the ordinary calendar from year to year. Ask where that second calendar comes from, and much of the answer is one chapter. Leviticus 23 lays out the sacred year from beginning to end, in forty-four verses. The great festivals a Jewish family keeps today have their roots here; Hanukkah and Purim came later.
screen: `TWO CALENDARS AT ONCE.` → `HOLIDAYS THAT WANDER.` → `ONE CHAPTER, FORTY-FOUR VERSES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. The chapter opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The appointed seasons of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations". In Hebrew, mo'adim. A mo'ed is a set time, an appointment. The Tent of Meeting, where God meets Moses, is the ohel mo'ed: same root. A holiday, in this picture, is a date God keeps with the people. Second, the list. Shabbat comes first, every seventh day. Then Passover and the week of matzah in spring. The first sheaf of barley, the omer, and seven weeks counted to Shavuot. Then the seventh month: a day of blowing the horn, which became Rosh Hashanah; Yom Kippur on the tenth; and Sukkot, the festival of booths, on the fifteenth. Third, who sets the date. The verse says these are the times ye shall proclaim. The Talmud tells of a dispute over when a month began, and reads the word for them, otam, as if it said atem, you: the people's court fixes the calendar, even if it errs. God's appointments, the rabbis taught, are kept on the people's calendar. Fourth, the rhythm. The year in Leviticus 23 isn't a list of days off. Spring is freedom, early summer is gift, fall is judgment, forgiveness and joy. It gives time a shape, so a year isn't one long run of the same day. Appointed times.
screen: `MO'ED: AN APPOINTMENT.` · `SHABBAT, SPRING, SUMMER, FALL.` · `ATEM: YOU SET THE DATE.` · `TIME GIVEN A SHAPE.` · then, large: `APPOINTED TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the next holiday on your calendar. Settle, and breathe. Think about your year. Which days stand out, and which blur together? Now think of the next holiday that matters to you, whatever it is: a Jewish festival, a family day, an anniversary. After the bell, put it on your calendar, and add one thing you'll do to keep the appointment: a meal, a call, a candle, a walk. The bell holds the time.
Mo'adim. Appointed times: the sacred calendar of Leviticus 23, from Shabbat through Passover, Shavuot, the new year, Yom Kippur and Sukkot.
Your line: appointed times. Today, put one appointment with something that matters into your calendar, and treat it like a meeting you can't miss. Day four hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: The Jewish calendar follows Leviticus 23's festivals on a lunar-solar year fixed by rabbinic calculation; Leviticus 22–23 is read in synagogue on several festivals, and some Jewish homes keep a Hebrew calendar beside the ordinary one.

fork.setup: a court proclaims a new month, and someone argues the date was wrong. whose date counts, in the Talmud's reading?
fork.reveal: the times ye shall proclaim: the Talmud reads it as you, even if you err. the people keep God's appointments on their own calendar.

original.note: Hebrew: appointed times, set seasons; singular mo'ed (Leviticus 23:2).

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of holidays.
what it means: appointments between God and the people, set on the people's calendar.
what a scholar hears: Rosh Hashanah 25a reads otam in Leviticus 23:4 as atem, giving the court authority even in error; 'Rosh Hashanah' as a name for the day comes from the Mishnah.

sources.quoted: The appointed seasons of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 23:2 'The appointed seasons of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations' quoted from memory; confirm.
Rosh Hashanah 25a (Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua; otam read as atem, from Lev 23:4): the script says 'the times ye shall proclaim' generally; confirm framing.
'Spring is freedom, early summer is gift (Torah at Shavuot), fall is judgment, forgiveness and joy' is a teaching summary; Shavuot as the giving of the Torah is rabbinic, not stated in Lev 23.
howItsDone: Lev 22:26–23:44 is read on the first days of Passover and Sukkot; confirm.

Editor review (y2 judaism 407–425): festivals also appear in Exodus 23, Numbers 28–29 and Deuteronomy 16, so 'the answer is mostly one chapter' is now 'much of the answer'; cut the 365-day figure (the Hebrew year is not 365 days); 'many Jewish homes' softened.
